newsitem.title: USA: Dow industrials weak at midday, tech stocks rally.
newsitem.headline: Dow industrials weak at midday, tech stocks rally.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Friday following a sell-off in bonds triggered by the March jobs report and another drop in International Business Machines Corp. stock.

At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 43.05 points, or 0.66 percent, at 6,434,30 after an initial sell-off drove the blue-chip index down more than 70 points to 6,404.84, below its 1997 start of 6,448.27.
In the broader market, declines led advances by a 13-10 margin on active New York Stock Exchange trading of 341 million shares.
Despite IBM's fall, high-tech stocks rallied as investors' perceptions of a strong economy raised expectations for earnings.
The Nasdaq Composite Index, a barometer of high-tech stocks, was up 11.46 points, or 0.94 percent, at 1,225.22.

Treasury bonds were down, with the key 30-year bond off 29/32, or $9.06 on a $1,000 bond, sending its yield up to 7.15 percent vs. 7.07 percent Thursday. Bond yields move in the opposite direction of prices.

The sell-off in bonds was prompted by the release of the eagerly awaited March employment report, which analysts said did nothing to dispel the belief that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates again, at or before the May 20 meeting of its policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).

"We were a little surprised at reaction in the bond market to the employment report. We thought it was mixed, not all that negative," said Anthony O'Bryan, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "But when the market is in this kind of mood, it looks at everything negatively. Good news is bad news. Bad news is bad news."

Economists surveyed by Reuters had forecast an unemployment rate of 5.2 percent and a rise of 196,000 in non-farm payrolls. While the 175,000 jobs created last month was below forecasts, workers' earnings have been edging upward.

In March, average hourly wages rose by 5 cents to $12.15, after edging up a revised 5 cents in February, instead of the previously reported 3 cents, the department said. Over the past 12 months, wages rose 4 percent, matching their highest growth rate since the 12 months ended June 1990, it said.
IBM shares were down 2-3/8 at 129 after Merrill Lynch cut its near-term rating on the stock to neutral from buy, keeping it a long-term buy.
Other high-tech stocks rallied, with Intel Corp. up 2 at 142-5/8, Cisco Systems Inc. was up 1-7/8 at 50-1/4 and Applied Materials Inc. was up 3-1/4 at 51-3/4.

"There are two sides to the coin," O'Bryan said. "A strong economy puts pressure on rates and raises inflation fears. On the other hand, it helps the techs, which are basically cyclical growth stocks and need a strong economy to keep the ball rolling."
Three brokerages downgraded Checkpoint Systems Inc., which was the most actively traded NYSE issue, falling 7-1/4 to 9-7/8.
